genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman described runs the kitchen of a country inn
she took her first steps at a very cramped cooking station
at the outset she followed written instructions to the letter
she weighed every ingredient then and dreaded getting it wrong
she now trusts her palate rather than a timer
she has given up fierce heat and favours a very gentle simmer
her former manner leant on a profusion of aromatics
her present manner leans on the worth of the raw material
she passes this change on to the beginners she trains regularly
she holds that mastery of the hand comes before mastery of waiting
text: The woman who runs the kitchen of a country inn learnt her trade at a very cramped little stove. In those early months she followed written instructions to the letter, weighed out every ingredient and lived in constant fear of getting something wrong. She trusts her own tongue now, and pays no attention at all to a timer. The fierce heat has gone as well: she keeps the pot barely trembling, because gentleness draws out flavours that haste destroys. What separates the two cooks she has been is not the skill of her hands. Her old way leant on a great heap of aromatics; her present way leans on the worth of what she buys. She hands that shift on to the beginners who come to her for training, and she tells them the same thing every time: the hand is mastered long before the waiting is.

units: the place described stands beside a waterway
the staff bring the dishes discreetly and without explanation
the list of dishes is short and fits on a single sheet
that list changes according to what the suppliers bring
the brevity of the offer suggests nothing is stored for long
the methods of cooking are not of constant quality
the fish is a success on the surface as well as inside
the root vegetables are spoilt by too heavy an accompaniment
the final sweet dish repairs the impression left by the vegetables
the conclusion recommends a visit despite an excess of sauce
text: Three things stand out in this dining room beside a waterway. The service is plain to an unusual degree. Plates arrive, nobody says a single word about them, and the diner is left to work out what is on the plate. The menu comes next. It fits onto one single sheet of paper and shifts with whatever the suppliers bring, and so little is offered that nothing can be sitting in a cold store for long. The cooking is where the kitchen wavers. The fish leaves the pan crisp on the outside and yielding within, while the roots, buried under a thick sauce, lose all their edge. The last course puts that right: a smooth cream, barely sweetened, with a fruit poached in its own juice. The place is well worth the journey, provided you accept that the sauce sometimes takes up more room than it should.

units: the writer of the message recounts a cooking experience of the day before
he browned sliced bulbs in a flat pan
he stirred without stopping so that the fat would not blacken
he then added pulses and water
the dish cooked gently while he cleaned up
the first attempt had no flavour at all
he corrected the seasoning with a sour fruit and crushed seeds
he covered the dish with a soured milk product
someone living in the same building went back three times
the writer admits he improvised the dish with no model
text: You will never guess what I got up to in my tiny kitchen late last night. I began by browning sliced onions in a wide flat pan, stirring the whole time so the fat would not catch and blacken. In went the lentils, then cold water over the top, and I left it all ticking over gently while I dealt with the washing up. Then I tasted it. Nothing. No flavour at all. So I squeezed in a good deal of sharp citrus juice, threw in a pinch of crushed seeds, and the whole pot woke up. I poured off the extra liquid, spooned soured milk over the lot and carried it to the table without much hope. My neighbour from upstairs, asked round at the last minute, went back for a third helping and wanted the recipe. I had to admit I had made it up as I went along. Come round next week and I shall do it again.

units: the text explains where the golden tint of a bread crust comes from
the colour is born of an interaction between sugars and proteins
very dry air sets that interaction off
a pale surface signals an oven that is not hot enough
too much water in the dough also delays the colouring
damp keeps the surface from reaching the temperature required
excessive heat turns the sugars black
that drift brings a bitter taste
a very dark crust is not necessarily a fault
the same change yields pleasant aromas and burnt ones alike
text: What gives a crust its amber colour? Apprentice bakers put that question constantly, and the answer lies in a meeting between the sugars and the proteins of the dough, set off by the dry heat inside the closed oven chamber. And when the surface stays pale? Usually the air is not fierce enough, or the dough carries too much water, and the steam holds the colour back, because damp keeps the surface below the point at which the reaction begins. What happens if the heat is pushed further still? The sugars caramelise, then they blacken, and bitterness settles in for good. Does a dark crust therefore betray a mistake made along the way? Not at all. The shade you aim for depends on the smell you want, since one and the same reaction yields the scent of toasted nuts and the smell of burning.

units: a trader in spices observes that his shop is declining
visitors smell the goods but leave with empty hands
their restraint comes from not knowing how to use these products
his pupil reckons that a scent alone does not bring about a purchase
she suggests setting a tasting pot on the counter
vegetables would steep in it in a scented liquid
the trader fears at first that there is no room
he ends by accepting the proposal
sales rise from the following week
visitors come back asking more precise questions
text: One wet evening the spice seller complained that his shop was dying for want of custom. He told his apprentice that people came in, leant over the jars, breathed deeply, then went out again with nothing, put off by powders they had no idea how to use. A smell on its own persuades nobody, she answered, not when it belongs to no particular dish. Why not keep a pot at one end of the counter, she said, with roots steeping in a scented broth, so that anyone could taste before buying? He hesitated, muttering about the room it would take, and then gave way. By the second week he admitted that the jars were emptying and that visitors came back with sharp, precise questions. His shop, he said with amused solemnity, had stopped selling powders and started selling ideas for supper.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the text contrasts two great methods of preserving food that came before mechanical cold
the first method consists in drawing the water out of food
salt, sugar and exposure to dry air belong to that method
depriving micro-organisms of water prevents them from multiplying
the second method changes the matter by souring or fermenting it
the ferments themselves create surroundings hostile to germs
drawing out water stiffens the texture and forces a soaking before use
the change alters the taste of the product markedly
it brings out aromas the raw matter never held
cold halts spoiling without enriching the flavour
text: Long before mechanical cold, two families of technique competed to keep food edible, and setting them side by side still explains a good deal about the way we cook. The first works by taking away. Salt, sugar and drying in open air pull the water out of the tissues and leave micro-organisms without the medium they depend on. The second works by changing the food itself. It is steeped in a sour brine, or handed over to ferments that build their own surroundings, hostile to any intruder. Taking water away hardens the texture and forces a long soak before use. Changing the food goes further and rewrites its flavour, sharpening it, rounding it, raising scents the raw matter never held. Cold came later. It halts decay and creates nothing, which explains both its reign and its blandness.

units: the text sets out four ways of carrying heat in cooking
boiling water spreads an even and limited heat
it softens the tough parts and draws out the soluble aromas
cooking by steam avoids washing the substances out of the food
it keeps the colour and the firmness of vegetables
a heated fat reaches a temperature higher than that of water
it serves to colour the surface before the heat is lowered
the dry heat of the closed chamber dries the outside and concentrates the sugars
the piece must be moistened with its own cooking liquid
linking these methods in a considered order gives results no single one can reach
text: Four ways of carrying heat cover very nearly everything that is done in a domestic kitchen, and each obeys a logic of its own. Boiling water gives an even, moderate warmth that can climb no higher. It softens tough tissue, dissolves the aromas that will dissolve, and suits any dish meant to yield a broth. Steam is gentler still, and it cooks without washing the food, so vegetables keep their colour and their bite. Hot fat carries far more heat than water ever can, which is why it is used to colour a surface before the flame is turned down. The dry air of a closed oven dries the outside and concentrates the sugars, so long as the joint is moistened now and then with its own juices. Set these four ways in a considered order and you reach textures that none of them ever reaches alone.

units: a large wedding reception is threatened by an accident of cooking
the cook in charge of the sauces left her pan on a source of heat
she had gone away to tend an assistant hurt in the hand
the bottom of the pan had become covered with a blackened deposit
the guests were already waiting to be served
she recovered the deposit by pouring pale wine over it
the deposit gave off a smell of nuts
she strained the liquid and enriched it with a cold fat
a relative of the bride asked how it had been done
she refused to set the method down in writing
text: A wedding feast came close to collapse because of a forgotten pan. The cook in charge of the sauces had left her reduction on a hot plate while she saw to an apprentice who had opened his finger on a blade. She came back to a dark sticky crust on the bottom of the pan, and the guests were already seated. Rather than start again, she poured in a glass of pale wine, scraped the base with a spatula and found that the burnt layer was giving off an unexpected smell of toasted nuts. She strained the liquid, beat in a knob of cold butter and sent it out without a word to anyone. The bride's father asked how it had been done before the pudding arrived. She told the tale to her colleagues at length, yet she would not write the method down, on the grounds that an accident cannot be ordered.

units: the instructions concern the cooking of a whole farmyard bird
it must be taken out of the cold well before it is cooked
without that rest the outside would be done before the middle
the skin must be wiped because water blocks the colouring
as long as water is evaporating the surface does not grow hot enough
the bird must be set on a support with holes in it
laid in its own juice the underside would cook in water
the piece must be moistened with its fat while it cooks
a rest after cooking is needed before carving
carving too soon loses the liquid and dries the flesh
text: Take a whole bird and get it out of the cold a good while before you mean to cook it, or the outside will be done long before the middle has even warmed through. Wipe the skin properly dry with a cloth, because damp stops it browning: while water is still evaporating, the surface never climbs to the temperature that turns it golden. Salt the skin generously, then sit the bird on a rack, never flat in its own juices, or the underside boils instead of roasting. Baste it with its own fat as it cooks, since hot liquid carries heat into the hollows the air struggles to reach. Then let the bird rest away from the heat for a while before you carve. The fibres tighten in the heat and give their juices back as they cool, and if you cut too soon it all runs onto the board and the meat comes out dry.

units: quantities of damaged vegetables were thrown away at the end of the market
the traders regretted that loss without being able to prevent it
the goods were still fit to eat despite how they looked
no arrangement allowed them to be recovered before closing
a group of local residents put forward an answer in three steps
the unsold goods are gathered just before closing
a room made available by the local authority is used for sorting
the vegetables are cooked and put into jars the same evening
the preparations are handed to households named by the social services
the lack of space and the absence of refrigerated equipment hold the project back
text: Whole crates of battered vegetables went into the skip week after week when the covered market shut, under the eyes of traders who minded but could do nothing about it. The produce was sound, merely bruised or a little too ripe to sell, and no arrangement existed for taking it away before nightfall. A group of residents from the neighbourhood came up with an answer in three moves: gather the unsold crates in the last hour of trading, sort them in a room lent by the local authority, and turn them into soup and preserves straight away. Volunteers simmer the vegetables that same evening, sterilise the jars and pass them on to families sent their way by the social services. Space is now the real sticking point. The room they were lent is full to bursting, and there is still no cold store to be had.
